To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the thermal consequences of impacts in an early solar system body depend on the internal temperature structure and the mass fraction of materials that were heated by the impact.
the thermal consequences of collisions between early solar system planetesimals depend on the internal temperature structure and the thermal properties of the target body prior to the impact event.

(1) impacts between planetesimals during the first 100 Myr in solar system history were not responsible for the thermal processing seen in the most highly metamorphosed meteorites, (2) the thermal consequences of impacts in this early epoch in the solar system's history were to accelerate the cooling of a planetesimal's interior, and (3) the thermal consequences are a function of the preimpact internal temperature structure of a planetesimal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the thermal evolution of a planetesimal that is impacted by another planetesimal.
the effects of impact events on the thermal history of a planetesimal in the early solar-system.

the thermal consequences of impacts in early solar system history, and we find that while collisions led to the heating around the point of the impact, a greater mass had its cooling rate accelerated as a result.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
impacts in the early, hot solar system did not lead to the global heating of meteorite parent bodies.
the thermal consequences of impacts in early solar system bodies were to accelerate the cooling of a greater amount of the mass of a body.
collisions in the solar system's early epoch led to the thermal evolution of the impacted body, but not necessarily the reverse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the thermal consequences of a single impact event on the thermal structure of a target body are negligible, although the thermal structure of the target is strongly dependent on the internal thermal structure of the body prior to impact.

collisions in the early, hot solar system were not responsible for the heating of the majority of mass in a target body, but they could be responsible for the heating and acceleration of the cooling rate of a significant fraction of mass.

impacts in the early Solar System were a more important factor in accelerating the cooling of the planetesimal population than they were for heating it, and thus the thermal evolution of the planetesimal populations in the early solar System were not significantly different from those of the present day.
The main takeaway from our work is that

impacts in the early inner solar system were a significant source of thermal processing for the materials within the impacted body and should be considered when attempting to model the thermal history of any meteorite parent body.

the thermal consequences of an impact in the early solar planetesimal disk depend strongly on the internal temperature structure prior to the collision, and this in turn is a function of the initial composition of the body, its size, and its distance from the Sun.
, for a given impact event, the thermal consequences of the impact depend on the thermal state of the target body prior to the event.
